title: Eid al-Fitr: the takbir
hook: on the way to Eid prayer, Allah is greatest, sung aloud

segments.voice: Yesterday, the whole book, and your line was one juz' a night. What steady step did you take on your long thing? Day five hundred eleven, the end of the week.

The crescent moon has been sighted, or the announcement has come through. Ramadan is over. The next morning, early, families are up in their best clothes. Kids in new shoes. Someone is handing out dates at the door. And from the mosque, from the open field where the prayer will be held, from people walking down the street in twos and threes, comes one phrase, sung over and over, in a melody many Muslims learned as children: Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar. Today, the sound of Eid morning.

The phrase is the takbir, from the root k-b-r, to be great. Allahu akbar: God is greater, God is greatest. Takbirat is the plural: the takbirs. On Eid al-Fitr, they fill the morning. Many scholars connect the practice with the end of the very verse we heard three days ago about Ramadan. It closes by saying God wants ease for you, and wants you to complete the count of days, and in Pickthall's words, "that ye should magnify Allah for having guided you". Magnify, there, is the same verb, tukabbiru: to say God is great. So the fast ends, the count is complete, and the first thing to do is the takbir. A common form goes: Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar, la ilaha illallah, wallahu akbar, Allahu akbar, wa lillahil hamd. God is greatest, God is greatest, there is no god but God, God is greatest, God is greatest, and to God belongs all praise. The wording and the number of repetitions vary a little between schools and regions. Then come small things the hadith preserve. Bukhari reports that the Prophet ﷺ wouldn't go out on the morning of Eid al-Fitr until he'd eaten some dates, an odd number of them. He went to the prayer by one road and came back by another; scholars give several reasons, and a common one is that more people would see and greet him. The charity of the fast, zakat al-fitr, was to be given before the prayer, so the poor could celebrate too. And in the Eid prayer itself there are extra takbirs, in many schools with raised hands, their number differing between schools. A month of quiet effort ends out loud.
screen: `K-B-R: TO BE GREAT.` · `MAGNIFY GOD FOR GUIDING YOU.` · `DATES, AN ODD NUMBER.` · `ONE ROAD THERE, ANOTHER BACK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say the Eid takbir. Sit, and let the breath settle. If you pray, say the takbir quietly, in Arabic or English, a few times through, and let it get a little stronger each time. If you don't, just listen to the words in your head, or picture the street on Eid morning: the clothes, the dates, the voices, the crowd heading the same way. The bell holds the time.
Takbirat. The takbirs, Allahu akbar, God is greatest, sung aloud on the way to the Eid prayer and called out within it. Today's word.

Your line: allahu akbar on the way. This week went from the Mawlid and the night journey, through Sha'ban and Ramadan, to Eid. Today, take a different road home, and greet someone on it. Day five hundred eleven.

howItsDone: On Eid al-Fitr, Muslims give zakat al-fitr before the prayer, often eat a few dates, and recite the takbir aloud on the way to the congregational Eid prayer, which includes extra takbirs; the wording and count vary by school.

original.note: Arabic: takbirat, the takbirs, saying Allahu akbar; from the root k-b-r, to be great.

trapdoor: what you thought: Allahu akbar is a phrase said in prayer.
what it means: on Eid, it's sung aloud on the way to the prayer, answering the verse that says to magnify God for guiding you through the month.

what a scholar hears: 'wa li-tukabbiru llaha 'ala ma hadakum' (2:185); Bukhari 953 (dates), 986 (two roads), 1503 (zakat al-fitr before the prayer); the count of extra takbirs differs, e.g. Hanafi and Shafi'i practice.
